tagline.text: Leyte's twin-towered cathedral that survived Typhoon Yolanda, and its memorial garden

location.label: Location
location.text: Palo, Leyte (along the coastal highway south of Tacloban)

children.text: The seat of the Archdiocese of Palo in Leyte began as a Jesuit mission in 1596 and became known worldwide through Typhoon Yolanda in 2013 and Pope Francis's visit in 2015. Its twin-towered façade and memorial garden are close to Tacloban and fit easily into a half-day trip.
The cathedral's official name is the Metropolitan Cathedral of Our Lord's Transfiguration. It stands on the coastal road of the town of Palo in northeastern Leyte, about
12km
south of central Tacloban. With its yellow-and-white walls and two tall bell towers, it is easy to spot from a distance and serves as the main church of the Archdiocese of Palo.

Its roots go back to 1596, when Jesuit missionaries traveled from Dulag to Palo and began their mission; the first church was built in 1598. In 1768, after the Jesuits were expelled from Spanish territories, the Augustinians took over the stone church, and in 1843 the Franciscans took charge of the parish. In November 1937 Palo became a diocese covering all of Leyte, the church was declared a cathedral on March 25, 1938, and Msgr. Manuel Mascariñas became its first bishop. In 1982 Palo was raised to an archdiocese. The first church, opened on August 15, 1598 (the Feast of the Assumption), was dedicated to Our Lady, and its early history was far from smooth: after a raid in 1613 the Jesuit residence moved to nearby Dagami. In 1926 the large rectory served as an apostolic and minor seminary, and in 1954 the Philippine Historical Committee designated the area a historic zone.

The cathedral appears in the history books twice. First, during World War II, from October 1944 to March 1945, during the Battle of Leyte, American forces used the building as a field hospital and refuge. The second time was Super Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) on November 8, 2013. The roof and ceiling were torn away and the stained glass shattered, but the thick walls stood and sheltered residents, and the grounds beside the church became a mass burial site for the victims. In November 2013 priests were ordained in the roofless church, and on Christmas Eve that year a papal legate celebrated midnight Mass here.

On January 17, 2015, during his visit to the Philippines, Pope Francis came here, met survivors and clergy, and prayed at the mass grave. Today the restoration is complete and it is an active church hosting regular Masses, weddings, and retreats, with tidy gardens that are pleasant for a quiet walk. Many travelers combine it with the MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial and the San Juanico Bridge on a Tacloban itinerary. The patron is the Transfigured Christ (Señor San Salvador), and the seating capacity is known to be about 1,200. A renovation costing about ₱25 million was carried out for the diocese's 75th anniversary in 2012, and in 2015 it was designated a pilgrim church for the Extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy.

The façade, with two tall towers rising above yellow-and-white walls, is the signature view. The building blends Spanish colonial and modern styles, and the view from the coastal road is the best known. The colors look richest in the morning and late afternoon when the sun is low.

Beside the church are a mass burial site for typhoon victims and a garden. Figures for the number buried vary by source, so an exact count is hard to state. It is a place of remembrance before it is a sightseeing spot, so walk quietly and show respect.

On January 17, 2015, the pope stayed briefly, met survivors' families and clergy, and prayed at the mass grave. It is said that a tropical storm was approaching, so the schedule was shortened. You can see photos and notices commemorating the visit in and around the church.

Above the choir loft is a Kimball pipe organ (Opus 6718) donated from the United States. The instrument has three keyboards and more than 1,000 pipes, and its installation was completed by 2015. It may be played during Mass, so timing your visit to a service gives you a chance to hear it.

blocks.title: A history that endured war and disaster

children.text: It served as an American field hospital during the Battle of Leyte in 1944, and in 2013 it became a roofless shelter. Few buildings have lived through both a war and a typhoon, so it is a good place to understand Leyte's modern history in one stop.

Masses are held on Sundays and weekdays at this active church. There are separate services in the local language (Bisaya) and in English, and some travelers who are not worshippers quietly observe from the back. Schedules change, so confirm with the parish before you go.
The garden has an angel statue, and the church grounds include a chapel where a weekday noon English Mass is held. It is a pleasant shady place to rest from the midday heat.

Every Good Friday, a Passion play known as the Pamalandong, which sings and meditates on the suffering of Jesus, is held around the church. Visiting during Holy Week lets you see local faith traditions up close, but crowds are heavy, so check the schedule and transport in advance.
Set out from central Tacloban by jeepney or taxi to Palo. The ride takes about
20–30 minutes
Arrive at Palo Cathedral, photograph the twin-tower façade first, then go inside to see the altar and the pipe organ.
Walk quietly through the memorial garden and the mass burial site beside the church.
Take a tricycle to the MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial to see the bronze statues and the beach.
Return to Tacloban for lunch and continue to the Santo Niño Shrine or the San Juanico Bridge.
Viewing inside the church may be limited during Mass, so check the schedule before you go. During Holy Week, pilgrimage events across Leyte crowd the roads, so book lodging and transport early.
There are direct flights from Manila (NAIA) to Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport (TAC) in Tacloban, taking about
1 hour 15 minutes–1 hour 25 minutes
. One-way fares range from about
There are also direct flights from Cebu taking about
50 minutes–1 hour
. Fares and schedules vary by season, so check when booking.
The cathedral is about
8.5km
in a straight line from the airport, and a taxi or hired car is the easiest way. Negotiate the fare or check whether the meter is used.
To go by jeepney, transfer in central Tacloban to a jeepney signed "Tacloban–Palo." Some older reviews mention fares of around
each for the airport to downtown and downtown to Palo, so confirm the fare locally.
Take a jeepney or van toward Palo or Tanauan; the ride takes about
20–30 minutes
. Tell the driver to drop you in front of Palo Cathedral.
The MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial is close to the cathedral and can be reached by tricycle.
Long-distance buses from Cubao in Manila to Tacloban go through Bicol and take a ferry, taking about
22–28 hours
. Recommended only if you have plenty of time.
Eastern Visayas faces the Pacific and gets plenty of rain. The cathedral can be enjoyed both inside and out, but the outdoor garden and exterior photos are better on clear days.
July–December is the typhoon season, when flight cancellations and flooded roads can occur. Leave a spare day in your schedule.

The church is busier than usual on Catholic observances. On Good Friday, Christmas Eve Mass, and around the November 8 typhoon remembrance, many local worshippers gather. If you want a quiet visit, avoid these dates; if you want to feel the local atmosphere, aim for them. Event schedules change every year, so check the latest announcements.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
Palo is a small town, so lodging and restaurants cluster in central Tacloban. Small hotels in the center cost about
a night, and mid-range hotels along the airport-side coastal road and near the malls run about
. If you only want to see the church, base yourself in Tacloban and make a day trip.

In Leyte, try snacks such as binagol, made of taro and coconut, and moron, glutinous rice and chocolate steamed in banana leaf. As a coastal city, it has many restaurants serving grilled fish and squid and kinilaw, a raw-fish ceviche.
Stalls selling snacks and drinks sometimes set up along the road in front of the church, but a proper meal is better had in central Tacloban. Carry enough cash and use an ATM beforehand.
Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees inside the church. Even if no dress code is posted, it is a place of worship, so it is best to show respect.
Sunday mornings can be crowded with Mass. To look around quietly, aim for the gaps between weekday morning Masses.
At the mass burial site, avoid loud voices and smiling photos, and give up photographing if the mood is not right.
Mass schedules change. Check the latest announcements, and confirm the parish contact locally.
Tricycles and stalls often take only cash, so carry small change.
Combining it with the MacArthur Leyte Landing Memorial on the same day keeps travel short and efficient. The memorial park is about
3km
away in a straight line.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and water, and walk the garden in the morning or late afternoon.
Speak softly inside the church even outside Mass, and avoid flash photography. The pipe organ above the choir loft sounds best during Mass.
On a day trip from Tacloban, head back before the return jeepneys stop running. Late in the evening there are fewer rides, and you may need to negotiate a taxi or tricycle.
This is an active church that commemorates typhoon victims before it is a tourist site. Behave quietly during Mass and remembrance, and check the latest announcements.
Viewing and photography may be restricted during Mass. Do not disturb worship.
During the July–December typhoon season, flights may be cancelled and roads flooded.
Vehicles often do not use meters, so agree on a price before you get in.
Mosquitoes are numerous in the rainy season, so watch for dengue and bring repellent.
Opening hours for the church have not been officially confirmed, so check locally before planning your day.
